title: Road Trip Average Speed Calculator
description: Calculate a trip's true average speed from distance and elapsed time with the Road Trip Average Speed Calculator — stops in or out. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 850 miles in 14 hours door-to-door averages 60.7 mph — while the same trip's moving average, over 12½ hours of wheels-turning, is 68 mph. Both are true; they answer different questions.
quick_answer: The Road Trip Average Speed Calculator divides a trip's total distance by its time and returns the average speed actually achieved. Enter the miles and the hours — elapsed for the honest door-to-door figure, moving for the driving figure — and read the speed your next trip plan should assume.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
Average speed: total distance ÷ total time, in mph and km/h — over elapsed time or moving time, whichever you enter.
Do I need an account?
No. Distance and hours in, average out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
For planning calibrations and log audits, yes — it is the exact division behind every fleet's average. Commercial tachograph rules are a separate legal layer.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Your time already contains the traffic you met; the calculator reports what it did to your average.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Enter the road distance you drove — dividing crow miles by real hours invents a slowness you did not suffer.
Elapsed or moving time — which is right?
Both, for different questions: elapsed for arrival honesty, moving for driving performance. This page's example shows them side by side for a reason.
Why is my average below the speed limit?
Towns, junctions, fuel and humanity. The limit is a maximum for moments; the average is the biography of the whole journey.
Why do fleets care about this number?
It sets schedules that are achievable rather than aspirational. A rota built on a 41 mph average survives; one built on the limit does not.
My car's trip computer shows higher.
It usually reports moving average and resets flatteringly. Your elapsed division over a known distance is the audit.
Same route, winter versus summer?
Expect a lower winter figure — light, weather and tyres. Keep seasonal averages and the plans inherit the seasons.
